title: 1 Maccabees
subtitle: a priest's sons, a defiled Temple, and the family that won Judea its freedom
lead: 1 Maccabees tells how the Jews of Judea rose against the Greek kings of Syria and won their freedom, in the forty years from 175 to 134 BC. King Antiochus IV Epiphanes plunders the Temple, bans circumcision, the Sabbath and the food laws, and sets up "an abomination of desolation on the altar" (1:54). An old priest, Mattathias, refuses to sacrifice to idols at his town of Modein, kills the king's officer, and flees to the hills with his five sons. His son Judas, called Maccabeus, wins battle after battle, cleanses the Temple and dedicates it again with an eight-day feast, the first Hanukkah (4:36–59). After Judas falls, his brothers Jonathan and Simon lead the people, play rival claimants to the Syrian throne against each other, make friends with Rome and Sparta, and become high priests. Under Simon "the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from Israel" (13:41), and the people name him leader and high priest "until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41). The book ends with Simon's murder and his son John taking his place. It has 16 chapters and 924 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox churches include 1 Maccabees in their Old Testament; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, "of the second canon." The Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches read it too, but the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches do not: their "Books of Maccabees" (Meqabyan) are different works. Protestants place it among the Apocrypha: Lutheran and Anglican Bibles long printed it between the Testaments, to be read for example of life but not to set doctrine, and Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches give it no authority. It is not in the Jewish Bible, though it is the oldest and fullest account of the events Jews remember at Hanukkah. Most scholars read it as a history written in Hebrew in Judea around 100 BC by a supporter of the ruling Hasmonean family, valuable and largely trustworthy, but written to honor that family.
facts: The Catholic Church (on the lists of Hippo, Carthage and Florence; defined at Trent, 1546), the Eastern Orthodox churches (named at Jerusalem, 1672; some Orthodox teachers rank it below the Hebrew books), and the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches by long use. Among the Apocrypha for Lutherans and Anglicans (read, not used for doctrine). Not Scripture for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches (whose Meqabyan are other books), for Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.

Unknown. The book never names its writer. Most scholars think of a Judean Jew, loyal to the Temple and the Law and a strong supporter of the Hasmonean family, perhaps connected with its court, since he knew its documents and records (14:27; 16:23–24).

Most scholars: about 130–90 BC, after John Hyrcanus became high priest in 134 BC and before the Romans took Jerusalem in 63 BC. The book's last verses speak of the record of John's high priesthood as if it were finished or well along (16:23–24), and it speaks warmly of Rome, which suggests a time before Pompey. Many date it around 100 BC, late in John's reign (134–104 BC) or early in that of Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC).

Judea and its neighbors from the accession of Antiochus IV in the year 137 of the Seleucid era (175 BC; 1:10) to the murder of Simon in the year 177 (134 BC; 16:14). A short opening (1:1–9) runs from Alexander the Great to the kings who followed him.
Judea, almost certainly Jerusalem: the writer knows the land closely and centers everything on the Temple and the Law.
Hebrew, now lost. Jerome says he found "the first book of Maccabees" in Hebrew, and Origen gives its Semitic title, Sarbēth Sabanaiel. The Greek reads like a close translation of Hebrew.

Greek, in Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), and in later manuscripts including those of the Lucianic (Antiochene) revision; Codex Vaticanus lacks the books of Maccabees. The Old Latin, which the Latin Vulgate took over unrevised by Jerome; Syriac and Armenian translations. No copy was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

A history in the style of the books of Samuel and Kings, with laments and poems of praise (1:25–28; 1:36–40; 2:7–13; 3:3–9; 3:45; 9:21; 14:4–15), speeches and prayers, and many letters, treaties and decrees quoted in full (8:23–32; 10:18–20, 25–45; 12:6–23; 14:20–23, 27–45; 15:2–9, 16–21)
authorship: Early Christian and Jewish readers did not name an author. Medieval Jewish tradition, as Saadia Gaon (900s) reports for the related Aramaic Scroll of Antiochus, credited the story to the Hasmoneans themselves, the sons of Mattathias. Christian writers usually treated the book as a faithful history written soon after the events, by a Jew of Judea, in Hebrew. Florentine Bechtel's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) is typical of the older Catholic view: the author is unknown, wrote in the last years of the 100s BC, and is a historian of the highest value, though inexact about the Romans.

Most scholars today agree on the main points. The author was a Judean of the Hasmonean court circle or close to it, writing in Hebrew in the style of Israel's historical books, in the generation after Simon. He had access to official documents and to written records of the family (16:23–24) and perhaps to a lost life of Judas (9:22). He wrote to show that the family of Mattathias was the one through which God gave Israel salvation (5:62), and so had the right to rule as high priests. Jonathan Goldstein dates the book to the reign of Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC); John Bartlett suggests about 110–90 BC; others place it earlier in John Hyrcanus's reign.

Some scholars have asked whether chapters 14–16 were added later, because Josephus, who follows 1 Maccabees closely in his Antiquities, stops using it around 13:42 and tells Simon's and John's story from other sources. Most scholars think the book is a unity and that Josephus simply preferred another source, or had a shorter copy; the question is open.

audience.to: Jews of Judea under the Hasmonean high priests, the heirs of Mattathias, in the generation after Simon (about 130–90 BC). Many of them could remember, or had heard from their parents, the persecution of Antiochus IV and the years of war. Their rulers were now high priests, generals and ethnarchs, and soon kings, though they were not descended from David and not from the old high-priestly line of Zadok. Some Jews opposed them for that reason, or for their wars and their worldly power: the Dead Sea Scrolls attack a "Wicked Priest" whom many scholars identify with Jonathan or Simon. The book was written in Hebrew for these readers. It was translated into Greek, probably soon after, and Josephus was reading it in Greek in Rome by the AD 90s.
audience.why: The writer wanted his readers to remember how close Israel had come to losing its Law and its Temple, and who had saved them. In his account God gives salvation through one family: Mattathias's zeal is like Phinehas's (2:26, 54), Judas fights like the judges and like David, and when other men try to win glory without them they fail, because "they were not of the seed of those men by whose hand Israel was given salvation" (5:62). The book shows the people choosing Simon as leader and high priest by public decree (14:27–47), so the family's rule rests on its deeds and the people's consent, "until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41). It also urges loyalty to the Law, zeal against those who abandon it, and trust in "Heaven," the help that comes from God. Knowing the readers changes the reading. 1 Maccabees is not a neutral chronicle. It is the founding story of a dynasty, told by one of its supporters, and much of what it stresses or leaves out serves that purpose.
views: Most scholars, such as Goldstein, Bartlett and Doran, read the book as written to support the dynasty's claim to rule, perhaps from its own circle. On this view the stress on Mattathias's family as God's chosen agents and on the people's decree for Simon answers those who doubted the family's right to the high priesthood.
An early or a later date

Scholars who date the book early in John Hyrcanus's reign see it as a defense of a new dynasty's founding. Those who date it under Alexander Jannaeus, whose rule was bitterly opposed by many Jews, see a writer looking back to the heroic founders to support a contested present.
A history for all faithful Jews

Some readers, ancient and modern, stress less the propaganda and more the call to faithfulness. The book honors all who "accepted death rather than be made unclean by food and profane the holy covenant" (1:63), and Mattathias's dying speech (2:49–68) calls every generation to zeal for the Law.

For the churches that read it as Scripture, the readers include the church, which hears in the book a call to stand by God's covenant under persecution. The Catholic lectionary reads it in the Mass for persecuted Christians and at the dedication of an altar.

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts 1 Maccabees among the deuterocanonical books, defined as Scripture at the Council of Trent (1546), and reads it as inspired history of God's faithfulness in the Maccabean revolt.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern Orthodox churches, and the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches, read 1 Maccabees in their Old Testament, from the Septuagint. The Ethiopian Orthodox Bible's three books of Meqabyan are different works.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place 1 Maccabees among the Apocrypha. Many Protestant teachers have prized it as the best history of the years between the Testaments while denying it the authority of Scripture.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 1 Maccabees as a pro-Hasmonean history written in Hebrew in Judea around 100 BC, valuable and largely reliable, and shaped to show the Hasmonean family as God's chosen saviors of Israel.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: 1 Maccabees is not in the Jewish Bible, and the rabbis told the Hanukkah story with the miracle of the oil rather than from this book; but it is the main source for the events Hanukkah remembers.

sections.b:
Read it first as history, in the manner of the books of Samuel and Kings, which the writer imitates on purpose. Like them it moves from leader to leader (Mattathias, Judas, Jonathan, Simon, John), dates events by the year, sets laments and songs of praise into the story (1:25–28; 3:3–9; 9:21; 14:4–15), and closes a life with the old formula about "the rest" of a leader's story and where it is written (9:22; 16:23–24; compare 1 Kings 11:41). The writer is telling the next chapter of Israel's history in the old style.

Then notice how the story is built. Chapters 1–2 are the crisis and the call: the Law banned, the Temple defiled, and Mattathias's zeal. Chapters 3–9 are the war of Judas, with the cleansing of the Temple at the center (4:36–59). Chapters 9–16 are the slow winning of independence by Jonathan and Simon, more by diplomacy than by battle, ending in Simon's peace, "each one sat under his vine and his fig tree" (14:12), the words of the prophets for Israel's golden age (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4).

Watch the documents. The writer quotes letters, treaties and decrees in full, from kings, from Rome and Sparta, and from the people of Judea. They give the book much of its historical value, and they are also his argument: foreign powers and Israel itself recognize the family's rule.

And watch what the book does not say. It never calls God "God" or "Lord" in Codex Alexandrinus, the text this site translates; it says "Heaven." It tells of no miracles and no angels, and it says nothing of life after death. Compare 2 Maccabees, which tells many of the same events very differently (see "Two books about the same war").

The Plain English is translated for this site from the Greek, as printed by H. B. Swete (1912), who prints Codex Alexandrinus (A), since Codex Vaticanus lacks the books of Maccabees, and gives the readings of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Codex Venetus (V) in his notes. The variant notes report where those manuscripts, the Lucianic text, the Old Latin and the Latin Vulgate differ in ways that matter, as scholars report them.

The Hebrew original is lost, so the Greek is the oldest text. Where the Greek seems to misread a Hebrew word, the notes say so. The King James Version's Apocrypha and the Douay-Rheims Bible, which translates the Latin Vulgate and spells the name "Machabees," were used only to check the sense. Names use the usual English forms (Mattathias, Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan, Simon, Antiochus Epiphanes, Modein, the Hasideans, Kislev), with the Greek in a note the first time where it differs. Dates are kept as the book gives them, in years of "the kingdom of the Greeks" (1:10), the Seleucid era, with the date BC in the notes.

Zeal for the Law. The crisis is not only foreign. It begins with Jews who say, "let us make a covenant with the nations around us" (1:11), who build a gymnasium in Jerusalem and hide their circumcision (1:14–15). Against them stands Mattathias, who is "zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been" (2:26). His dying charge sets the book's ideal: "be zealous for the law, and give your lives for the covenant of our ancestors" (2:50). The same zeal kills Jewish apostates as well as foreign soldiers (2:24, 44), which raises hard questions the chapter pages discuss.

The Law kept and the Law adapted. The faithful die rather than eat unclean food (1:62–63), and a thousand let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath (2:29–38). Then Mattathias and his friends decide that they will fight if attacked on the Sabbath, so that the faithful will not all die (2:41). The book shows Israel's leaders deciding how to keep the Law in a crisis, and it lays up the stones of the defiled altar "until a prophet should come to give a ruling about them" (4:46).

One family chosen to save. Judas, Jonathan and Simon are Israel's saviors, and the book says outright that others who fought without them failed (5:55–62). The people's decree for Simon (14:27–47) is the climax.

Heaven fights for the few. "Winning a war is not a matter of how big an army is. Strength comes from Heaven" (3:19). Judas prays before battle (3:44–54; 4:30–33; 7:40–42) and recalls David and Jonathan (4:30), but God acts through the fighters, not by signs.

Israel among the nations. The book admires Rome and makes treaties with it (8; 12:1–4; 14:16–19; 15:15–24) and claims kinship with Sparta (12:6–23). In its story the Seleucid kings are treacherous, and the safety of Judea lies in faithfulness at home and wise friendships abroad.

sections.h: Two books about the same war
sections.b:
2 Maccabees, also in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, is a different book, not a sequel. It is a Greek summary of a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene, covering about 180–161 BC, and it overlaps with 1 Maccabees 1–7. The two differ in ways that matter to the churches:

  • The family. 1 Maccabees honors the whole house of Mattathias and makes it Israel's saving dynasty. 2 Maccabees centers on Judas alone, never mentions Mattathias, and gives the brothers little place; it honors the high priest Onias III and the martyrs.
  • The high priests. 2 Maccabees names and condemns the Hellenizing high priests Jason and Menelaus (2 Maccabees 4). 1 Maccabees never names them, and blames "renegades" and the king (1:11–15).
  • Miracles and angels. 2 Maccabees is full of them: heavenly riders at the Temple (2 Maccabees 3:24–28), armies in the sky (2 Maccabees 5:2–4), radiant horsemen leading Judas (2 Maccabees 10:29–30; 2 Maccabees 11:8), and a vision of Jeremiah giving Judas a golden sword (2 Maccabees 15:12–16). 1 Maccabees has none.
  • The resurrection. In 2 Maccabees the martyred brothers die in hope that God will raise them (2 Maccabees 7:9, 14), and Judas has an offering made for the dead in view of the resurrection (2 Maccabees 12:43–45), the passage Catholics cite for prayer for the dead. 1 Maccabees says nothing of life after death. Its dead win "glory" and a lasting name (2:51; 9:10).
  • Dates and order. 1 Maccabees puts the death of Antiochus IV after the Temple was cleansed (4:52; 6:16); 2 Maccabees puts it before (2 Maccabees 9–10). It uses a different start for the year, so some dates differ by one.
  • Hanukkah. 1 Maccabees tells of the eight-day dedication (4:56–59); 2 Maccabees adds that it was kept like the Feast of Booths (2 Maccabees 10:6–7). Neither mentions the miracle of the oil, which first appears in rabbinic sources (the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b, and the later commentary on the Scroll of Fasts).

Scholars of all traditions use the two books together, usually preferring 1 Maccabees for the order of events and 2 Maccabees for the years before the revolt.

In Jewish memory. The book is the oldest account of how Hanukkah began: Judas and the assembly of Israel decided that "the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept at their season every year, for eight days" (4:59). Josephus, about AD 94, retold the story from 1 Maccabees and said the feast was called "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325). The Aramaic Scroll of Fasts (Megillat Ta'anit, first century AD), a list of days on which fasting was forbidden, includes the eight days from 25 Kislev, the Day of Nicanor (13 Adar; 7:49) and, as the notes on 13:51–52 explain, the day the Citadel was taken. The rabbis did not keep the book. The Babylonian Talmud explains Hanukkah instead by the miracle of a single jar of pure oil that burned for eight days (Shabbat 21b). The Aramaic Scroll of Antiochus, which Saadia Gaon (900s) first mentions and which copies passages from 1 Maccabees, was read on Hanukkah in some Italian and Yemenite communities, as Louis Ginzberg reports.

In Catholic worship. The Catholic lectionary reads 1 Maccabees on four weekdays of the 33rd week in Ordinary Time (Year I): Antiochus's persecution (1:10–15, 41–43, 54–57, 62–63), Mattathias's refusal (2:15–29), the dedication of the Temple (4:36–37, 52–59) and the death of Antiochus (6:1–13). It also offers 2:49–52, 57–64 in the Mass for persecuted Christians (Lectionary 877) and 4:52–59 at the dedication of an altar (Lectionary 817).

In the Orthodox churches 1 Maccabees is part of the Old Testament, read from the Septuagint. The feast of the Holy Maccabees (August 1) honors the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, not the heroes of this book; we have found no source for regular readings from 1 Maccabees in the Byzantine services.

In art and music. Judas Maccabeus became a model of the Christian knight: he is one of the medieval Nine Worthies, and Handel's oratorio Judas Maccabaeus (1747) made him familiar to Protestant England.

• Maccabeus (Greek Makkabaios), the surname of Judas (2:4), later used for the whole family and the books. Its meaning is uncertain: most connect it with Hebrew maqqebet, "hammer."
  • Hasmoneans, the family's later name, from an ancestor Hasmon (Josephus); 1 Maccabees does not use it.
  • Mattathias, a priest of the family of Joarib (2:1), and his sons John, Simon, Judas, Eleazar and Jonathan (2:2–5).
  • Antiochus IV Epiphanes, "God made manifest," king of the Seleucid empire, 175–164 BC.
  • Hasideans (Greek Asidaioi, Hebrew ḥasidim, "the loyal ones"), a group devoted to the Law who joined the revolt (2:42; 7:13).
  • The abomination of desolation (1:54), the pagan altar set on the altar of burnt offering in 167 BC, in Daniel's words (Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11).
  • Kittim (1:1), a name for peoples of the west, here the Macedonians; in Daniel 11:30 the ships of Kittim are usually taken as the Romans.
  • The kingdom of the Greeks (1:10), the Seleucid era, counted from 312/311 BC.
  • Heaven, the book's usual way of naming God (3:18–19; 4:24, 55; 12:15; 16:3).
  • Kislev, the ninth month (November–December), when the altar was defiled (1:54) and dedicated again (4:52).

spec.title: Claude's theory: two things laid up until a prophet comes
spec.body: The book twice puts a question aside "until a prophet" comes. The stones of the defiled altar are stored on the Temple mount "until a prophet should come to give a ruling about them" (4:46), and Simon is made leader and high priest "forever, until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41). Commentators often set these verses side by side with 9:27 as evidence that prophecy was thought to have ceased. My suggestion is that the writer uses them as a frame for the whole story of the dynasty: the first is about the old altar, which was holy but defiled, and the second about the new rulers, who were not of David's or Zadok's line. In both, the leaders of Israel do the best they can under the Law and leave the last word to God. Read this way, the book's defense of the Hasmoneans is a modest one: their high priesthood is real and lawful, but it waits, like the old stones, for a word from God.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Mattathias's roll call and the faith chapter of Hebrews
spec.body: Mattathias's dying speech (2:51–60) is a roll call of heroes who kept faith in testing: Abraham, Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, David, Elijah, the three in the fire, and Daniel in the lions' den. Hebrews 11 is a longer roll call of the same kind, and in Hebrews 11:33–34 the lions' mouths and the power of fire come together, as in 2:59–60, followed by people who grew strong in battle and turned back foreign armies. Scholars have long compared such lists (Sirach 44–50 is another). My suggestion is that Hebrews may have known this kind of Maccabean roll call, with its pairing of Daniel and the three, and turned its moral around: Mattathias calls his sons to glory and an everlasting name (2:51), while Hebrews says that all these died without receiving the promise (Hebrews 11:39–40). This is a guess about the form of the lists, not a claim that Hebrews quotes 1 Maccabees.

views: Yes. 1 Maccabees is one of the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament. "Two books of Maccabees" are on the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) and of Pope Innocent I (405), and the Council of Florence (1442) named them. The Council of Trent (1546) defined the whole list, two books of the Maccabees, the first and the second, included, as sacred and canonical, with an anathema on anyone who rejects it, and the Catechism (120) lists 1 and 2 Maccabees. Catholic writers answer the argument from 9:27 that inspiration does not require a prophet's office (see the next card).

Yes, in the Old Testament, though Orthodox teachers explain its rank in two ways. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85, late 300s), which the Council in Trullo (692) received, list "three of the Maccabees," and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named "the Maccabees" among the "genuine parts of Scripture." The Orthodox Church in America's answer counts the books of Maccabees "fully part of the Old Testament." But the Russian theologian Michael Pomazansky, following Athanasius's shorter list, calls the three books of Maccabees non-canonical, accepted as "useful and instructive."

Yes for the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches, by long use. A Coptic Orthodox diocese's teaching page lists 1 and 2 Maccabees among the deuterocanonical books the Egyptian church received. These churches never held a council like Trent to define the list.

Not this book. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches count three "Books of Maccabees" (Meqabyan) in their 81-book Bible, but R. W. Cowley reports that these are not the same as any of the Greek books of Maccabees; they tell other stories altogether.

Not Scripture, but good to read, and highly valued. Luther's Bible put 1 Maccabees with the Apocrypha between the Testaments, as books not held equal to Holy Scripture yet useful and good to read. His preface (1533) says the book is not in the Hebrew Bible, yet its words and speech keep the style of the other books of Scripture, and it is very necessary and helpful for understanding Daniel 11; in his preface to 2 Maccabees he says it would be proper for the first book to be included among the sacred Scriptures. Lutheran confessions never fixed the canon; Martin Chemnitz taught that such books may not be used to prove doctrine.

Not canonical, but read. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "the First Book of Maccabees" among the books that "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine," quoting Jerome. The King James Version printed it with the Apocrypha.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture," and are to be used only as other human writings. The Belgic Confession (article 6) names "the two books of Maccabees" among books the church may read for instruction where they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm any point of faith.

No. The Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration, while still citing some of these books. When an inquisitor cited 2 Maccabees (12:43) for prayers for the dead, the martyr Jacques d'Auchy answered that "they are not authentic books from which a rule or ordinance might be taken."
No. John Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) kept the Anglican list of canonical books but left out the paragraph that names the Apocrypha, so 1 Maccabees has no place in Methodist doctrine.

No. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.2–3) lists the 66 books and nearly repeats Westminster: the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Many Baptists and other evangelicals still value 1 Maccabees as the best history of the years between the Testaments.

No. Evangelical writers often add an argument from the book itself: as Norman Geisler puts it, "Maccabees disclaims being prophetic (1 Macc. 9:27)," since it says prophets were no longer seen in Israel. Roger Beckwith and F. F. Bruce argue that Jesus and the apostles received the Hebrew Bible of the Jews, which did not include it.

traditions.q: Does the book's statement that prophets were no longer seen rule it out?
views: Yes, it is a strong sign. Many evangelical writers hold that Old Testament Scripture was written by prophets, that prophecy ceased after Malachi until John the Baptist, and that Jewish sources agree: Josephus says the later writings were not trusted equally "because of the failure of the exact succession of the prophets," and the rabbis said the holy spirit of prophecy had departed. A book that says no prophet was seen in its own day (9:27) and that its leaders waited for one (4:46; 14:41) testifies against its own place in the canon, as Geisler argues.

Yes, in its older form. The Reformed and Presbyterian argument is that the Old Testament canon closed when inspiration ceased with the last prophets. Archibald Alexander (1826), defending the Westminster position, wrote that these books were written "long after the time of Ezra and Malachi" and in Greek, a language "not known to the Jews, until long after inspiration had ceased, and the Canon of the Old Testament was closed," and that Josephus's nation received only twenty-two inspired books. He does not cite 9:27 itself; later Protestant writers add it as the book's own admission.

No. Catholic writers answer, first, that the verses describe the time of the events, not the writer's own claim about his book: they show the people expecting a prophet to come, as Charles Grondin puts it. Second, inspiration is not the same as the office of a prophet: much of the Old Testament comes from writers who were not prophets or are unknown. Third, earlier times without prophets (1 Samuel 3:1; Psalm 74:9; Lamentations 2:9) did not stop God from inspiring Scripture. Fourth, the Maccabean age itself records revelation: Judas's dream of the high priest Onias and the prophet Jeremiah (2 Maccabees 15:11–16), and 4:46 and 14:41 show the people expecting prophecy to return, not a door closed for good. And God spoke again through Simeon and Anna before John the Baptist (Luke 2:25–38), as Jimmy Akin argues.

canon.summary: 1 Maccabees is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox churches, and is read by the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, and some Orthodox teachers rank it below the Hebrew books. It is not in the Ethiopian Bible, whose "Books of Maccabees" are other works. Lutherans and Anglicans place it among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, and it is not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books. Augustine counted the two books of the Maccabees in the canon (On Christian Teaching 2.8.13) and wrote that the books of the Maccabees are held as canonical "not by the Jews, but by the Church" (City of God 18.36). The books are on the list of the Council of Hippo (393), repeated at Carthage (397), and in Pope Innocent I's letter to Exsuperius (405). The Council of Florence (1442), in its decree of union with the Copts, listed them. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 1546) defined the list, two books of the Maccabees, the first and the second, included, as sacred and canonical, receiving all its books "with an equal affection of piety and reverence," and the Catechism (120) names 1 and 2 Maccabees. The Latin text was the Old Latin, which the Vulgate kept unrevised. 1 Maccabees is read at Mass on weekdays of the 33rd week in Ordinary Time (Year I), in the Mass for persecuted Christians, and at the dedication of an altar.

In the Old Testament, which the Orthodox read in the Greek of the Septuagint, with 2 and 3 Maccabees (and 4 Maccabees in an appendix in Greek Bibles). Its rank has been explained in two ways. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85, late 300s), received by the Council in Trullo (692), list "three of the Maccabees" among the books of the Old Testament, and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), answering Protestant ideas, named "the Maccabees" among the "genuine parts of Scripture." The Orthodox Church in America's answer calls these books "fully part of the Old Testament." Yet Athanasius's list (367) does not name the Maccabees at all, even among the books "to be read," and the Russian theologian Michael Pomazansky counts the three books of Maccabees among the non-canonical books, accepted as "useful and instructive." Kallistos Ware reports that most Orthodox scholars today give these books a lower footing than the rest.

In their Old Testament by long use. A Coptic Orthodox diocese's teaching page lists 1 and 2 Maccabees among the deuterocanonical books that the Egyptian church accepted, and links the feast of Dedication in the Gospel with Judas Maccabeus. Syriac and Armenian translations of the book exist; Louis Ginzberg thought the Aramaic Scroll of Antiochus copied it from the Syriac. These churches never held a council like Trent to define the list. The Assyrian Church of the East is not covered here.
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches

Not this book. Their 81-book Bible has three books called Maccabees (Meqabyan), but Cowley reports that they are "not the same as any of the 4 LXX books of Maccabees": the first tells of a Benjaminite named Meqabis who taught the worship of the true God. The church law book Fetha Nagast lists "Machabees, two books" without saying which books are meant, and Cowley notes that the same tradition counts the book of Joseph son of Koryon (the medieval Hebrew Josippon) as "(another) book of Machabees." So the lens and the canon notes on this site that speak of "Oriental Orthodox" use of 1 Maccabees do not include the Ethiopian church.

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (Latin 1563, English 1571) names "the First Book of Maccabees" among the other books that, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The King James Version (1611) printed it with the Apocrypha. Modern Anglican provinces differ in how much they read it.

Among the Apocrypha, and praised above most of them. Luther's complete Bible (1534) gathered these books between the Testaments as books not held equal to Holy Scripture, yet useful and good to read. His preface to 1 Maccabees (1533) says that it is not in the Hebrew Bible, yet keeps the style of the other books of Scripture, and is very necessary and helpful for understanding Daniel 11, so it is good for Christians to read and know. His preface to 2 Maccabees adds that it is proper for the first book to be included among the sacred Scriptures, while the second should be thrown out. Lutheran confessions never fixed a canon; Martin Chemnitz (1565–73) taught that such books may not prove doctrine.

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 6) names "the two books of Maccabees" among the books the church may read and take instruction from as far as they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm faith. The Westminster Confession (1646) says the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon of the Scripture" and are not "to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings."

Not Scripture. The Global Anabaptist Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration, while Menno Simons and Dirk Philips often cited some of these books. The martyr Jacques d'Auchy, when an inquisitor cited 2 Maccabees (12:43) for prayers for the dead, valued the Apocrypha as edifying but said they are not books "from which a rule or ordinance might be taken."
Not Scripture. Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) took over the Anglican list of canonical books but dropped the paragraph naming the Apocrypha.

Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) nearly repeats Westminster's words, calling the Apocrypha "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Most evangelical churches hold the 66 books. Many evangelical teachers value 1 Maccabees as history of the years between the Testaments, and some, such as Norman Geisler, argue from 9:27 that the book itself disclaims being prophetic.

Not Scripture, and the book itself was not kept in Hebrew. 1 Maccabees is not in the Hebrew Bible, and the rabbis of the Mishnah and Talmud never name it. Origen (about 240) knew its Hebrew title, and Jerome (about 391) said he had found it in Hebrew, so a Hebrew text was still known; it has since been lost. Josephus (about AD 94) used it as his main source for these years (Antiquities 12–13). The rabbis remembered Hanukkah through the miracle of the oil (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 21b) rather than through this book. The Aramaic Scroll of Antiochus, which copies some passages of 1 Maccabees, was read on Hanukkah in some medieval communities. No copy of 1 Maccabees was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Read and valued, usually as Scripture in the West, with doubts in the East. Origen (about 240), listing the 22 books of the Hebrew canon, added that "outside these there are the Maccabees," and gave their Semitic title (Eusebius, Church History 6.25). Tertullian already used the book: he recalls that "in the times of the Maccabees" the Jews fought bravely on the Sabbath (An Answer to the Jews 4; compare 2:41). Writers who followed the Hebrew count placed it lower: Jerome (about 398) said the church reads "the books of the Maccabees" but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures; Rufinus (about 404) counted them among the "ecclesiastical" books read in church; Athanasius (367) and Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) left them out of their lists altogether. The Apostolic Canons listed three books of Maccabees, and the North African councils, Innocent I and Augustine counted two in the canon.

provenance.h: When and where it was written
provenance.b: The book was written in Judea after the events it tells, which end with Simon's murder in 134 BC and John Hyrcanus taking his father's place (16:11–24). Its last verses say that John's wars and deeds "are written in the book of the days of his high priesthood, from the time he became high priest after his father" (16:24), which sounds as if John's rule was finished, or at least long established. It speaks of Rome as a faithful friend (8:1–16), which most scholars think would be hard to write after Pompey captured Jerusalem in 63 BC. So most date it between about 130 and 90 BC. Many prefer about 100 BC, at the end of John's reign (134–104 BC) or under Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC); Jonathan Goldstein argued for Jannaeus's reign, John Bartlett for about 110–90 BC, and some scholars for a date early in John's reign.

The writer never names himself. Everything in the book points to a Judean Jew, devoted to the Temple and the Law, who admired the family of Mattathias without reserve. He knew the land closely, quoted official documents and the decree for Simon set up on bronze tablets on Mount Zion (14:26–49), and knew of a written record of John's high priesthood (16:24). He wrote in the style of the books of Samuel and Kings, which suggests he saw this as the next chapter of Israel's sacred history. Most scholars think he was connected with the Hasmonean court, or wrote to support it.

No Hebrew copy of 1 Maccabees survives, but ancient witnesses saw one. Origen, about 240, listing the books of the Hebrew Bible, added that "outside these there are the Maccabees," which were "entitled Sarbēth Sabanaiel" (as Eusebius quotes him, Church History 6.25). The title is Hebrew or Aramaic in Greek letters, and no one is sure what it means: its parts may include the words for "book," "house" or "dynasty," and "God," and proposals include "book of the prince of the house of Israel" and "book of the house of the Hasmoneans." Jerome, in his preface to Samuel and Kings (the Prologus galeatus, about 391), wrote that he found "the first book of the Maccabees" in Hebrew, while "the second is Greek, as can be proved from its very style." The Greek itself confirms a Hebrew original: it is full of Hebrew idioms and sentence patterns, and some odd Greek words are best explained as mistranslations of Hebrew.

The Greek, made from the Hebrew probably not long after the book was written, survives in three of the great codices: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), and in later minuscule manuscripts. Codex Vaticanus (B), the base of many Septuagint editions, has no books of Maccabees. Scholars also identify a Lucianic (Antiochene) form of the text, a revision found in several minuscules, which the Peshitta, the main Syriac version, follows, as Florentine Bechtel reports; a second Syriac version follows the ordinary Greek. Werner Kappler's Göttingen edition (1936; 3rd ed. 1990) is the standard critical text. Swete's edition, used for this site, prints Alexandrinus and reports Sinaiticus and Venetus in its notes. In Alexandrinus the book never calls Israel's God "God" or "Lord"; Sinaiticus and Venetus add "God" at 3:18, and Venetus reads "the sanctuary of the Lord" at 1:37.

The Old Latin (Vetus Latina) was made from the Greek in the early centuries and survives in more than one form. Jerome did not translate the books of Maccabees: the Latin Vulgate simply kept the Old Latin, which Bechtel describes as "probably unretouched by St. Jerome." That Latin was the Catholic 1 Maccabees for more than a thousand years, and the Douay-Rheims (1609–10) translated it. There are also Syriac and Armenian translations made from the Greek. In some places the Latin and Syriac seem to keep a better Greek reading than the codices, and scholars use them to correct the text.

Josephus, writing his Jewish Antiquities about AD 94, retold 1 Maccabees at length in books 12 and 13, often paraphrasing it closely and adding material from other sources, such as Nicolaus of Damascus. He follows it to about 13:42 and then tells Simon's and John's story from elsewhere. Whether his copy lacked chapters 14–16 or he simply preferred another source is unknown. Josephus is the first to say that Hanukkah was called "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325). After him, Jews did not keep the book, though medieval writers knew its story: the Aramaic Scroll of Antiochus, first mentioned by Saadia Gaon in the 900s, copies passages of it, and Louis Ginzberg thought from the Syriac version.

The book is written to honor one family. Mattathias acts with the zeal of Phinehas, who won "the covenant of a holy priesthood" (2:26, 54; Sinaiticus and Venetus read "an everlasting priesthood," the words of Numbers 25:13), a hint that his descendants have earned the high priesthood too. Judas is praised in a poem like a hero of the judges (3:3–9). Others who fight without the family fail, because "they were not of the seed of those men by whose hand Israel was given salvation" (5:62). Kings appoint Jonathan high priest (10:20–21), and the people confirm Simon as leader and high priest by a public decree (14:27–47). The family's failings get little space: Judas's alliance with Rome is praised, not questioned; the Hasideans who trusted the high priest Alcimus are shown as naive (7:12–18); the Hellenizing high priests Jason and Menelaus are not even named. Scholars call the book Hasmonean history or propaganda, and they mean it as a description of its purpose, not a judgment that it is untrue.

Compared with 2 Maccabees and with Daniel, 1 Maccabees is strikingly restrained about God. It names God as "Heaven" (3:18–19; 4:24, 55; 12:15; 16:3) or simply "he." Judas prays before battle and the people fast and read the Law (3:44–54), and they give the glory for victory to Heaven (4:24, 55), but the book tells of no heavenly riders, no angels and no visions. Nor does it speak of life after death. Mattathias promises his sons "great glory, glory that lasts forever" (2:51), meaning lasting fame, and Judas chooses to die "with courage" rather than "stain our glory" (9:10). The martyrs of 1:60–63 simply die. In 2 Maccabees, by contrast, the martyrs die in hope of being raised (2 Maccabees 7:9, 14), and Judas has an offering made for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43–45). Some scholars think the writer shared the outlook of the later Sadducees, who denied the resurrection; others think he simply wrote history in the manner of Kings, which also says little about the afterlife.

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
1 Maccabees is full of the Hebrew Bible, and these links run from the Hebrew Bible to 1 Maccabees, not the other way.

  • Samuel and Kings: the style, the dated reigns, the closing formulas (9:22; 16:23–24; 1 Kings 11:41), the lament for Judas, "How the warrior has fallen" (9:21; compare 2 Samuel 1:19), and Judas's prayer recalling David and Jonathan (4:30; 1 Samuel 14; 1 Samuel 17).
  • Numbers 25: Phinehas's zeal, the model for Mattathias (2:26, 54).
  • Deuteronomy 20: the rules for holy war, which Judas follows when he sends home the newly married, the builders and the fearful (3:56).
  • Daniel 7–12: the same crisis seen as prophecy. 1 Maccabees borrows Daniel's "abomination of desolation" (1:54; Daniel 11:31) and Mattathias recalls Daniel and the three in the fire (2:59–60).
  • Psalm 79: quoted at the murder of the Hasideans (7:17).
  • Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25: each under his vine and fig tree, in the praise of Simon (14:12).

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible has 24 books (the Christian Old Testament's 39 counted differently), and 1 Maccabees is not among them. Josephus, writing about AD 95, says the Jews have 22 books, written from Moses to the reign of Artaxerxes; the history written since then has not been trusted equally, "because of the failure of the exact succession of the prophets" (Against Apion 1.41). Josephus knew 1 Maccabees well and used it as a source, but he plainly did not count it among the 22. Origen likewise listed the Maccabees "outside" the Hebrew books. Protestants argue, in its strongest form, that the Old Testament was entrusted to Israel (Romans 3:2), that Jesus and the apostles used Israel's Scriptures, and that the New Testament never quotes 1 Maccabees. So the church should receive the books Israel received. Some earlier Catholic and Orthodox teachers drew a similar line: Jerome, and in Orthodoxy Athanasius's list and Pomazansky's dogmatics.

rejected_why.h: The book says prophecy had ceased
rejected_why.b:
1 Maccabees itself says three times that there was no prophet in its day. The stones of the defiled altar are stored "until a prophet should come to give a ruling about them" (4:46). After Judas's death Israel suffered distress "worse than any since the day a prophet was last seen among them" (9:27). And Simon is made leader and high priest "forever, until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41). Later Jewish teachers said the same of their whole age: Seder Olam says the prophets prophesied by the holy spirit until the time of Alexander the Great, and the Tosefta that when the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the holy spirit ceased from Israel (Tosefta Sotah 13:2–4; the numbering differs by edition).

The Protestant argument, in its strongest form. Reformed writers such as Archibald Alexander (1826) argued that the Apocrypha were written "long after the time of Ezra and Malachi," after inspiration had ceased and the canon was closed. The Old Testament Scriptures were given through prophets (Hebrews 1:1; 2 Peter 1:20–21; Luke 24:44). Josephus and the rabbis agree that the line of prophets ended in the Persian age, and Jesus himself speaks of the blood of the prophets "from Abel to Zechariah," the first and last martyrs of the Hebrew Bible in its Jewish order (Luke 11:51). 1 Maccabees, writing centuries later, admits that no prophet spoke in its time and that its leaders waited for one. It never claims to speak for God, never says "thus says the LORD," and even avoids God's name. A book that so honestly places itself outside the time of prophecy cannot, on this view, be part of the prophetic Scriptures, however true its history. Roger Beckwith gathers the Jewish evidence for the end of prophecy at length, and Norman Geisler puts the argument briefly: the book "disclaims being prophetic (1 Macc. 9:27)."

Jerome (about 347–420) made his Old Testament from the Hebrew, the Hebraica veritas, "Hebrew truth." In the preface to Samuel and Kings he said that what is outside the Hebrew books is to be set among the apocrypha, and in the same preface reported finding 1 Maccabees in Hebrew. In the preface to the books of Solomon he said the church reads Judith, Tobit and "the books of the Maccabees" but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, reading them for the building up of the people, not to confirm church doctrine. It is the sentence Article VI echoes ("as Hierome saith"). He never translated them. Athanasius (367) and Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) left the Maccabees out of their lists altogether, and Rufinus counted them among the "ecclesiastical" books. Augustine, by contrast, counted two books of Maccabees in the canon, and the North African councils followed him.

Protestant writers also point to features of the book that seem to set it apart from the canonical histories: its open praise of one family, its admiration for pagan Rome (8:1–16), and its errors about Rome's government (8:16) and about the peace with Antiochus III (8:6–8), set out under "How reliable is it?" Most of them do not doubt that its history is largely true. Their point is that being true and being Scripture are not the same: Luther and many Protestants valued 1 Maccabees as history while denying it the authority of the Word of God.

On the canon. Catholic teachers say the church received the Old Testament in Greek from the apostles' time, the Septuagint that the New Testament writers often quote, and that the canon was the church's to recognize, as Hippo, Carthage, Innocent I, Florence and Trent did. Augustine wrote that the books of the Maccabees are held canonical "not by the Jews, but by the Church." The Jewish canon was itself still debated in the first century, and the church did not take its list from the rabbis.

On the end of prophecy. Catholic writers answer the argument from 4:46, 9:27 and 14:41 in several ways. The verses describe the time of the events and the people's hope for a coming prophet; they do not say that God could inspire no book, as Charles Grondin argues. Inspiration is not the same as the office of a prophet: David and Solomon were kings, many historical books have unknown authors, and the church does not require that every inspired writer be a prophet. Times without prophets came before (1 Samuel 3:1; Psalm 74:9), and the period itself records a revelation to Judas in a dream (2 Maccabees 15:11–16); God still raised up prophets after it, such as Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:25–38) and John the Baptist, so there was no fixed "silence" that closed the canon, as Jimmy Akin argues.

On the book's limits. On the Catholic view a book written to honor a family can still be inspired history, as Chronicles honors David's house. The book's statements about Rome report what Judas heard ("Judas heard what the Romans were known for," 8:1), as Bechtel notes, not what the writer teaches.

Orthodox teachers do not appeal to Florence or Trent, which the East did not receive. They point to the Septuagint the church has always read, where the books of Maccabees stand among the histories; to the Apostolic Canons (canon 85), which list three books of Maccabees and which the Council in Trullo (692) received; and to the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), which named "the Maccabees" among the genuine parts of Scripture against the Calvinist confession of Cyril Lucaris. At the same time the Orthodox are open about their own division: some, like Pomazansky, follow Athanasius and the Hebrew count and call these books "useful and instructive" but not canonical, while others, like the Orthodox Church in America's answer, call them "fully part of the Old Testament." Both groups read 1 Maccabees in church as part of the Old Testament. We have found no Orthodox writer who argues the question of its inspiration from 9:27 one way or the other.

cited_in.b: John says that the feast of Dedication (Greek ta enkainia) came round in Jerusalem, in winter, and that Jesus was walking in the Temple, in Solomon's Portico. This is the feast whose founding 1 Maccabees tells: Judas and the assembly decided that "the days of the dedication of the altar" (enkainismos) be kept every year for eight days from the 25th of Kislev (4:59; compare 4:36, 56). It is the book's most certain point of contact with the New Testament, but it is a shared event, not a quotation: John names the feast, not the book. Commentators have long explained John's feast from 1 Maccabees 4 (for example the Cambridge Bible and Ellicott's commentary, citing 4:59), and the Coptic Orthodox page cited above links John's feast with Judas Maccabeus.

Hebrews lists people who by faith overcame kingdoms, closed lions' mouths, put out raging fire, grew strong in battle and turned back foreign armies (Hebrews 11:33–34), others who were tortured and turned down release to win a better resurrection (Hebrews 11:35), and others who roamed deserts and hills and lived in caves and holes in the ground (Hebrews 11:38). Most commentators connect 11:35 with the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, where the Greek word for the torture (tympanon) appears (2 Maccabees 6:19, 28). Some see the Maccabean wars as well in 11:34 and the flight to the hills and the hiding places in 11:38 (2:28–31; compare 2 Maccabees 5:27; 2 Maccabees 6:11). W. F. Moulton, in Ellicott's commentary (1880s), wrote that "no words could more truly characterise the general contents of the First Book" of Maccabees than Hebrews 11:34, and older commentaries such as Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Cambridge Bible cite 2:28–29 for the mountains and caves of 11:38. The lions and the fire (Hebrews 11:33–34) also come together in Mattathias's roll call (2:59–60), but both draw on Daniel. Hebrews names no book, so a link to 1 Maccabees is possible but disputed.

Jesus speaks of "the abomination of desolation" (Greek to bdelygma tēs erēmōseōs) standing in the holy place and tells those in Judea to flee to the mountains; Matthew names Daniel as the source. 1 Maccabees uses the same Greek phrase for the pagan altar that Antiochus's men built on the altar of burnt offering in December 167 BC (1:54), and tells how Mattathias and his sons fled to the hills (2:28). Both take the phrase from Daniel (Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11). 1 Maccabees is the earliest witness to reading Daniel's words as Antiochus's altar, and it shows how the phrase would have sounded to Jesus' hearers: a desecration like the one under Antiochus. The link runs through Daniel; the Gospels do not quote 1 Maccabees.

Mattathias asks, "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" (2:52). He joins Abraham's testing in the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) to the verse about faith reckoned as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). James makes the same join: Abraham was shown righteous when he offered Isaac, and so the Scripture was fulfilled that says he believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (James 2:21–23). Paul reads Genesis 15:6 apart from works (Romans 4:2–5). Hebrews too speaks of Abraham "tested" when he offered Isaac (Hebrews 11:17). Mattathias's line shows that the reading James uses was already common in Judaism (compare Sirach 44:20), as Irving Jacobs (1976) and Marion Soards (1987) point out. Shared tradition, not a quotation.

Priests and Levites ask John the Baptist, "Are you the Prophet?" (John 1:21), and the crowds say of Jesus that he is truly the Prophet who was to come (John 6:14; John 7:40). 1 Maccabees shows the same hope a century and a half earlier: the leaders of Israel set questions aside "until a prophet should come" (4:46) and "until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41). Both build on the promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18) and the return of Elijah (Malachi 4:5). The Cambridge Bible on John 1:21 already compares 14:41. Shared tradition.

Paul tells a man who was circumcised when called not to undo it (Greek mē epispasthō, the technical word for drawing a foreskin back over the place). 1 Maccabees tells how Jews in Jerusalem under Antiochus "made foreskins for themselves" (1:15), the earliest report of the practice. Commentators on 1 Corinthians, such as Meyer and Vincent, cite 1:15 to explain Paul's word. The link is a shared practice, not a quotation.

The crowd takes palm branches (Greek ta baia) and goes out to meet Jesus as he enters Jerusalem, praising him as the king of Israel. When Simon entered the Citadel he came in "with praise and palm branches" (baia), with lyres, cymbals and songs, "because a great enemy had been crushed and cast out of Israel" (13:51). Ellicott's commentary compares the word, and the Cambridge Bible compares Simon's triumphal entry. 2 Maccabees 10:7 has palms at the first Hanukkah too. Shared tradition: a Jewish way of greeting a victor, not a quotation.

Simon "the Zealot" among the Twelve (Luke 6:15), the believers in Jerusalem "all zealous for the law" (Acts 21:20), and Paul, who says he was extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Galatians 1:14; compare Philippians 3:6), all use the language of zeal that 1 Maccabees made a byword. Mattathias was "zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been" (2:26) and called out, "Everyone who is zealous for the law and stands by the covenant, come out and follow me!" (2:27). Martin Hengel traced the later Zealot movement's ideal of zeal through Phinehas and Mattathias. The New Testament does not cite the book, but its readers knew that ideal.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish faith in the century before Jesus, 1 Maccabees is very valuable: it shows how Judeans of the Hasmonean age understood the Law, the Temple, the Sabbath, martyrdom and zeal, and how they hoped for a prophet to come. As a text, it is good but second-hand: the Hebrew original is lost, and we read a close Greek translation preserved in three great codices and later manuscripts, with Latin and Syriac versions that sometimes help. As history, it is the best source we have for the years 175–134 BC. Its Seleucid dates fit the Babylonian records closely, its places and rulers are real, and many of its documents are widely accepted as genuine in substance, though some, above all the Spartan letters, are debated. It is also openly partisan: it is written to honor the Hasmonean family, and it is inexact about distant Rome and inflates some numbers. The churches that hold it as Scripture read it as true history told from a faithful point of view; Protestant churches mostly accept its history while denying it the authority of Scripture. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with their faith in the God who saves Israel and with the Law it defends, goes beyond them in some of its rulings and its ideal of zeal, and differs from the New Testament mainly in its silence about life after death and its warm view of Rome.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish faith before Jesus: high
sections.b: Here no church disagrees. Written within a generation or two of the events, by a Judean who lived among the people who fought them, 1 Maccabees shows: the Law as the center of Jewish identity, with circumcision, the Sabbath and the food laws as the points where it was attacked and defended (1:41–63); the scrolls of the Law burned and searched (1:56–57; 3:48); the Temple as the heart of the nation, cleansed and dedicated again (4:36–59); the willingness to die rather than break the covenant (1:62–63; 2:29–38); the debate over fighting on the Sabbath (2:41); the ideal of zeal modeled on Phinehas (2:26, 54); a body of "holy books" already in hand (12:9); and the expectation of a prophet to come (4:46; 14:41). It names the Hasideans (2:42; 7:13), one of the first Jewish religious groups we know of. It gives the earliest account of Hanukkah. For the Jewish world in which the New Testament was written, it is one of the most important sources there is.

Good in Greek, lost in the original. The Greek translation is close and literal, and survives in Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD), Alexandrinus (400s) and Venetus (700s) and in many later manuscripts, including a Lucianic revision. They differ in many small ways (word order, the spelling of names, a word added or left out), but they tell the same story in the same words. The Old Latin and the Syriac were made from the Greek and sometimes keep a better reading. The Hebrew was seen by Origen and Jerome and then lost; no fragment has been found, and none was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. So where the Greek seems to misread the Hebrew, the original can only be guessed. Josephus's paraphrase in Antiquities 12–13 is an early witness to the contents of chapters 1–13.

Where it is strong. Historians of every background regard 1 Maccabees as the most reliable source for the Maccabean revolt and the early Hasmonean state. Its rulers, from Antiochus IV to Antiochus VII, and their wars, rivalries and dates fit the Greek historians (Polybius, Diodorus) and the cuneiform records. A striking test: 1 Maccabees dates Antiochus's death to the year 149 of the Seleucid era (6:16), and a Babylonian king list (BM 35603, published by Sachs and Wiseman) records that in the year 148, in the month Kislev, it was heard that King Antiochus had died. The two fit closely once one allows for the different starting points of the Seleucid year; scholars broadly accept the book's dates, while debating whether it counts its years from spring 311 BC or autumn 312 BC and why it places Antiochus's death after the rededication (4:52) while 2 Maccabees places it before. Its geography of Judea and its battles are detailed and largely credible, as the military historian Bezalel Bar-Kochva's study of the battles shows, though scholars think some of the numbers are inflated.

Where it is weak. The writer is inexact about faraway Rome. He says the Romans took Antiochus III alive (8:7), but Antiochus was defeated at Magnesia (190 BC) and made peace at Apamea (188 BC), not captured; that they gave "India" and Media to Eumenes (8:8), though by the Peace of Apamea Antiochus lost only his lands west of the Taurus mountains; and that they entrust their rule each year to one man (8:16), though Rome had two consuls. The opening says Alexander divided his kingdom among his officers while still alive (1:6), a legend. Bechtel notes that in such places the writer reports what Judas heard, not his own claim.

The documents. The book quotes many letters and decrees. Most scholars accept the treaty with Rome (8:23–32) as genuine in substance; Ory Amitay, noting that it too has been attacked, calls the case against it "extreme hypercriticism." The decree for Simon (14:27–45) and the Seleucid letters are widely accepted too. The Spartan correspondence (12:6–23; 14:20–23) is the most debated: the letter of the Spartan king Areus to the high priest Onias, saying that Spartans and Jews are brothers descended from Abraham (12:20–23), has been doubted by Hadas, Hengel and others and defended by Goldstein, Katzoff and others, while Erich Gruen and Jan Bremmer have argued that the whole exchange is invented. Ory Amitay (2013), surveying the debate, argues for authenticity but admits that "any conclusions necessarily remain educated guesses."

The shaping. The book is partisan history. It tells the story so that the family of Mattathias earns the leadership, leaves out the Hellenizing high priests' names and much of the family's politics, and gives others' failures to show that salvation came only "by the hand" of this family (5:62). Most historians treat this as the writer's point of view rather than as invention of events.

The Catholic and Orthodox answer. The churches that read it as Scripture read it as history, as it presents itself. Catholic teaching on literary forms (Divino Afflante Spiritu; Dei Verbum 11–12) asks what the writer meant to assert. Bechtel, writing in 1910, already distinguished the author's own assertions from the reports and documents he passes on, so that a mistaken report about Rome is not an error of the author. The Orthodox churches have made no ruling on these questions known to us. A fair summary: the book is as reliable as any ancient history of its time, and more than most, but it should be read as the account of a loyal supporter of the dynasty.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: the one God who saves Israel and gives victory not by numbers but by his strength (3:18–19; 1 Samuel 14:6; Psalm 33:16–17); faithfulness to the covenant, the Sabbath, circumcision and the food laws (1:62–63; Exodus 31:13–17; Leviticus 11; Daniel 1:8); the Temple's holiness and its cleansing (4:36–59; 2 Chronicles 29); the hope for a prophet like Moses (4:46; 14:41; Deuteronomy 18:15–18); the heroes of faith from Abraham to Daniel (2:51–60); the events that Daniel 11 describes.
  • Goes beyond: (a) the decision to fight on the Sabbath when attacked (2:41), a ruling the Torah does not make, later accepted by the rabbis; (b) the new feast of Dedication (4:59) and the Day of Nicanor (7:49), added to the feasts of the Law, as Purim was (Esther 9:20–32); (c) the honor given to one priestly family as Israel's saviors, and the people's decree making Simon high priest "forever" (14:41), though the Hebrew Bible gives the high priesthood to Aaron's line through Phinehas and later Zadok (Numbers 25:13; Ezekiel 44:15).
  • Differs or may conflict: (a) Life after death. The book says nothing of the resurrection, which Daniel (Daniel 12:2) and the New Testament teach, and offers only lasting glory (2:51). This is a silence, not a denial. (b) Rome. The book praises Rome as a faithful friend (8:1–16); Revelation, as most interpreters read it, sees Rome as the beast and Babylon (Revelation 13; Revelation 17–18). (c) Zeal by the sword. Mattathias kills a fellow Jew at the altar and his followers strike down apostates (2:24–25, 44), on the model of Phinehas (Numbers 25:7–13); Jesus forbids his followers to take the sword for his cause (Matthew 26:52; John 18:36). (d) The silence of prophecy. The book's statement that no prophet was seen (9:27) agrees with the Jewish view of its age; Christians read the coming of John the Baptist and Jesus as the end of that silence (Luke 16:16).
  • Each church's view: Catholic and Orthodox churches read 1 Maccabees as Scripture in harmony with the rest of their Old Testament and the New: they read (a) as a silence that 2 Maccabees and the New Testament fill, (b) as a true picture of how Rome looked to Judas, (c) as an episode of Israel's history, judged by the whole of Scripture and by Christ, and (d) as a description of the time, not a disclaimer of inspiration (see the second card under "Where Christians differ"). Lutheran and Anglican churches read it as a good human book, useful for example of life and for understanding Daniel, never to establish doctrine. Reformed, Baptist and most evangelical churches value it as history, and see its silence on prophecy and its partisan character as signs that it is not inspired.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you are Catholic or Orthodox (but not Ethiopian Orthodox), 1 Maccabees is in your Bible, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide to it. If you are Protestant, it is not Scripture for you, though Luther called it very necessary for understanding Daniel and Anglican tradition commends it for example of life, and every reader can learn from it the history the New Testament assumes. Either way, read it with respect and with an eye to the differences on this page.

how_to_read.h: Read it as history from a point of view
how_to_read.b: Read 1 Maccabees as you would read the books of Kings: as a history with dates, places and documents, written by someone who believed God was at work in it and who had a clear view of who the heroes were. Ask what happened, and also why the writer tells it this way. Notice the documents, the speeches and the poems, and the places where the family's opponents are named or left unnamed.

how_to_read.h: Read it beside Daniel and 2 Maccabees
how_to_read.b: Read Daniel 11 before 1 Maccabees 1 and 6, and Daniel 9:27 and Daniel 12:11 beside 1:54. Daniel 11:21–35 describes, as a vision of the future, a despised king who wins power by intrigue, invades Egypt, turns against the holy covenant, profanes the sanctuary and stops the daily offering; nearly all interpreters, Jewish and Christian, see Antiochus IV there, and Luther wrote that 1 Maccabees is very necessary for understanding Daniel 11. Readers who date Daniel to the 500s BC read 1 Maccabees as the history that fulfills its prophecy; most critical scholars date Daniel 7–12 to the crisis itself, about 167–164 BC, so that the two books are two Jewish answers to the same events, and many take Daniel's "little help" given to the faithful (Daniel 11:34) as a cool reference to the Maccabean fighters (Collins). Then read 2 Maccabees 4–10 beside 1 Maccabees 1–7. You will see the same years told three ways: as prophecy, as sober history, and as history full of wonders and martyrs. The differences, set out under "Two books about the same war," matter for the resurrection, prayer for the dead and the role of miracles.

how_to_read.h: Read it as the background to the Gospels
how_to_read.b: Many things in the Gospels make more sense after 1 Maccabees: the feast of Dedication (John 10:22), the "abomination of desolation" (Mark 13:14), the hope for the Prophet (John 1:21), the palm branches of the entry into Jerusalem (John 12:13), the undoing of circumcision (1 Corinthians 7:18), the zeal of Simon the Zealot (Luke 6:15), the Sabbath debates, the high priests' power, and Rome's friendship turning to rule. Read John 10:22–39 after 1 Maccabees 4:36–59.

On the question whether a book that says prophecy had ceased can be Scripture, and on the book's zeal and violence, the churches give real answers, set out above and on the chapter pages. Read each in its strongest form before deciding.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "1 Maccabees, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants." Say which text you quote (Greek, or the Latin of the Douay-Rheims). It is the best single source for the years between the Testaments, the story behind Hanukkah, and a key to Daniel 11.
